text: There isn't an official description of how [product_name] handles block execution, but based on my observations and tests, here are some patterns: 1. Blocks are reviewed from lowest to highest repeatedly until all complete. 2. A block won't run if its input-linked blocks haven't yet run, and each block only executes once per cycle. 3. text: [product_name] operates similarly to larger PLCs. Step 1: Copies input states to the input register. Step 2: Runs the program using the input register values. Changes in input status during the cycle won't affect the program until the next cycle. While running the program, changing parameters update immediately (for instance, counter states, outputs, etc.). The program executes blocks from 001 onwards, but this isn’t documented and might not always be true. Step 3: Copies output statuses to the outputs. Step 4: Restarts from step 1. So, a change in physical input (or output) during the cycle only impacts the program in the following cycle. This explains the programming warning: 'Recursions of Input of xxxblock can only connect to output by a Marker or Output.'

text: [user_name], we seem to agree. When I mention block input from another block, I mean a link from one block’s output to another block’s input connection—not an input from the register. My rules fit well with your step 2. Here's an example using three blocks (numbered accordingly): - Block 001: Mathematical Instruction, V1 = 5 * Set OUTPUT: When En="0", output is Last Value. Otherwise, it won’t function correctly. - Block 002: AND(EDGE) (Simulates one program cycle) - Block 003: Mathematical Instruction, V2 = 10 * Set OUTPUT: When En="0", output is Last Value. Connections: - Input I1 links to Block 002's first input - EN input of Block 001 connects to Block 002's output - EN input of Block 003 connects to Block 002's output - Block 003's P1 parameter links to Block 001's Aq parameter - Block 001 output goes to AM1 - Block 003 output goes to AM2 Testing: 1. Reset all blocks to zero in the simulator. 2. Turn Input 1 on/off. AM1 reads 5, AM2 reads 10. Block 003: P1 = 5, P2 = 10, Aq = 10. Execution explanation: - Block 001 is reviewed first but waits as 002 hasn't executed. - Block 002 executes (linked only to input registers); its output goes HIGH. - Block 003 executes since 002 already did; Aq on Block 001 is still zero, so Block 003 adds 0 + 10 for 10. - Now, all blocks are executed, the cycle ends. Test another setup: - Create Block 004 (AND(EDGE)), remove Block 002 - Link I1 to Block 004's input - EN of Blocks 001 and 003 connect to Block 004's output Run the same test: AM1 reads 5, AM2 reads 15. Block 003: P1 = 5, P2 = 10, Aq = 15. Blocks 002 and 003 were skipped initially (since 004 hadn't executed). Block 004 ran after 003 was checked. On the second round, 002 and 003 executed because 004 was already done. This logic lets you predict block behavior. [product_name] might use a more advanced system internally, but this matches observable behavior.

text: VM memory addressing is organized by bytes. The smallest unit is a bit; 8 bits make up a byte. Two consecutive bytes (16 bits) make a word, and two consecutive words (4 bytes or 32 bits) form a double word. For example, V0.0 refers to bit 0 in byte 0. VB0 contains bits V0.0 to V0.7. VW0 includes VB0 and VB1 (bits V0.0 to V1.7), and VD0 includes VW0 and VW2 (VB0 to VB3 or V0.0 to V3.7). In bit addresses, the number before the dot is the byte address; the number after is the bit within that byte. For word and double word addresses, the number indicates where the sequence starts. To prevent overlap when working with words, always use even addresses (VW0, VW2, VW4, etc.), and for double words, use multiples of four (VW0, VW4, VW8, etc.).
